You wanna take that, Patrick?
Patrick Chaffin

Sure. Hey, Chris, this is Patrick Chaffin. Good to hear from you this morning. To your question, how we're pacing so far in Q1, you know, like the entertainment business, we had a little bit of a setback just from the weather in Nashville in January. Overall, the group trends continue to be encouraging. We are seeing groups that are showing up and signing up for a lot more food and beverage outside the room than they originally had anticipated. You know, I don't know that we'll see quite the outsized performance that we saw last year, but thus far, we are encouraged by what we've seen.
As far as how we're contracting going forward, you know, we continue to make sure that the inflationary pressures that we've all been feeling across the industry get priced into our food and beverage in real time. We are making sure that the pricing is appropriate and always trying to move folks to a higher food and beverage minimum. I would say there's been no material change in how contracting has gone forward thus far.
Chris Woronka
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Okay. Super helpful. Just as a quick follow-up, you mentioned and also at the investor day a lot of capital projects on the horizon. How are you thinking about prioritizing those based on whether it's ROI or just expected performance at a given property or market?
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. You wanna take that, Mark?
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. The way that we're looking at these, Chris, is one is based on ROI and the other is based on customer feedback in terms of what's important to the meeting planner and the attendee, the feedback we've gotten through not only primary research, but also the customer satisfaction scores that we receive, and then also, you know, ultimately managing construction disruption, you know, as we look at the various hotels, room renovations, et cetera, some of that timing is determined, you know, when is the best time to undertake those projects.
Chris Woronka
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Okay. Yeah, very helpful. Thanks.
Operator
Our next question will come from Dori Kesten with Wells Fargo.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
Thanks. Good morning. Given the phasing of renovations over the next few years, would you expect this year to be the most disruptive to earnings?
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I mean, if you look at the next two or three years, you'll have about the same level, I think, of disruption as we rotate through the portfolio with the various room renovations. You know, we've got three slated, I guess, for the next two years. I think that this year and next year would be your two most have the most amount of disruption, and I would guess about the same dollar amount.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Let me add to this. I mean, we can look at disruption, you know, as half empty, but the half full part of all of this is we're showing enormous growth in our hotel business. I suspect that we'll see in 2025 and 2026, as some of these projects start to come online, very, very good growth. It's just part of the price you have to pay for building, you know, superior demand into your business. We have this ability to grow our business materially, and we'll do that. We'll manage disruption just like we have over the last, you know, pick it, decade.
Patrick Chaffin
EVP and COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. Dori, this is Patrick.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
Right.
Patrick Chaffin
EVP and COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I would tell you that even on the Palms renovation, which is a 1,400-room renovation slated for this year that'll start in a few weeks, we're continuing to massage that schedule to make sure that when we see high demand opportunities to take advantage of, that we manage the design and construction process so that the tail's not wagging the dog, and that we're putting value creation first, even in the midst of this disruption.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. There's many, many times this year that that hotel with already its contracted book of business will be basically full.
Patrick Chaffin
EVP and COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Correct.
Colin Reed

We'll manage around that. This is the way we, you know, we've run this business over the last decade. We know how to do this. The real exciting thing is the underlying business that we have on the books for T+1, T+2. Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Dori, just one other point. You know, on the entertainment side, the projects that are creating the disruption this year will be completed this year. You know, we shouldn't have any next year, in that business.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yep.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
Right. I probably should have said net disruption. On Austin City Limits, can you walk through, I guess, what maybe what best practices from your national assets you've been able to instill there to drive results?
Patrick Moore
CEO, Opry Entertainment Group
Sure. No, this is Patrick Moore speaking. In the Investor Day, we outlined, you know, sort of our value creation program that we deploy across all of the venues. When you look at Austin City Limits, there's a number of factors that we're sort of pushing both the top and bottom line. For example, we brought food and beverage in-house. We are taking over some of the frontline staff that is outsourced. We are improving overall show count and driving sort of demand relative to pricing and dynamic pricing. We are looking at things like block booking and routing from some of the national-based assets into Austin. There's a number of factors across a range of areas that we're driving at ACL.
Two other ones that I would mention is first, we're redeveloping some of the areas between the hotel and Austin City Limits to have private events and other events before the show. I'd say the second thing is, like we have in other assets, we are driving a tour business that we expect to launch at the end of this year.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
Okay. If I can keep you, Patrick, would you expect majority of growth at OEG over the next few years can more come from your internal growth drivers, what you just talked about, and then just the projects that are ongoing, or is there a likelihood of external growth there?
Patrick Moore
CEO, Opry Entertainment Group
You know Austin specifically, Dori?
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
No, just for OEG.
Patrick Moore

Total. Yeah. For OEG in total, you know, we're putting three major projects online, Vegas, you know, Category Ten, which is gonna be, as Colin outlined, a significant upgrade to that property. Then obviously the improvements both to the W Austin and Austin City Limits. I would say that the short answer is, we're looking predominantly at the organic growth of the things that we have because we're putting so much capital into service. That being said, we're always looking for unit growth of our existing brands and other investment opportunities.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. I again, Patrick, I think, you know, in conversations yesterday with our board, you know, we talked about focusing on those new opportunities that are not embedded into our business today. Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
All right. Thank you all.
Patrick Moore
CEO, Opry Entertainment Group
Thanks, Dori.

Managing Director, Raymond James
Hey, good morning. Congrats on another year. Mark, I was wondering if you could address the National. You know, I would say relative to the rest of the portfolio, it has been slower to ramp, but what's really driving that, Bill, is the market. You know, the DC market has not recovered as quickly as the other markets that we're participating in. When you compare the National to itself and how it performed pre-pandemic, you know, that hotel has never performed better, whether you're looking at, you know, how they're performing with groups, group penetration, food and beverage revenues, food and beverage margins, you know, customer satisfaction scores. The other thing that I've noticed with the National, Patrick, you may wanna talk about this, is that just the pace of bookings that we've seen over the last 12 months; it's been very encouraging. Yeah, I would agree. I think we've reached that point now. While we, as we talked about at Investor Day, we're prioritizing Opryland, Rockies, and then our Texas hotels.

Bill Crow

That's great color. Exactly what I was looking for. If I could just do a follow-up, and I can't remember if this was addressed at the investor day or not. Patrick Chaffin

President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.

Yeah. Hey, this is Patrick. Let's start. There were a couple of questions there. We typically enter the year with about 50 points of occupancy on the books from a group perspective, and we book somewhere between 15-20 in the year for the year. We expect that will be consistent with this year. From a rate perspective, just to give you a sense of, let me break it down this way and see if this answers your question. Our RevPAR for 2024 assumes about a third of the growth. Our RevPAR growth assumes about a third of that's coming from occupancy and about two-thirds of it's coming from ADR growth. Our sales team is doing an outstanding job of pushing group rate. Jay Kornreich
VP, Wedbush Securities
That's very helpful. Thank you. Then just one other follow-up. You referenced fully overlaying the ICE! program on the JW Marriott Hill Country later this year in Q4. I was wondering if you can give any context as to the EBITDA contribution upside you believe that can provide.
Patrick Chaffin
EVP and COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
When we enter into a market with ICE! for the very first time, it takes a little while to build the customer base, if you will. We see it takes, you know, two-three years. However, given the fact that Dallas is only about four hours away, our analysis of the markets and the MSAs indicates to us that this could be a strong performer for us, so maybe a little bit better than what we would normally see. I would say that we believe there's somewhere between $3-5 million of revenue and profitability opportunity from putting ICE! in at this property in the first year, and we'll see how it goes.
Jay Kornreich
VP, Wedbush Securities
Okay. Thank you very much. That's it for me.
Patrick Chaffin
EVP and COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you.

Smedes Rose
Director, Citi
Hi. Thanks. I just wanted to circle back on, you talked about kind of the cadence of RevPAR growth over the course of the year. Are we right in thinking that Q1 will maybe be the weakest of the year, followed by Q4, with Q2 and Q3 being your best two quarters? Is that the right way to think about just kind of the seasonality of earnings?
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yes. That's correct, Smedes. You got that right.
Smedes Rose
Director, Citi
Okay. I was just also kind of wondering, you know, you talked a fair amount about the capital projects, and I know you're doing a fair amount of work at the Gaylord Rockies. I guess my question is this, the need to go in and kind of make the property more accommodated to groups, it seems like it's relatively new to have maybe misunderstood the market or to misunderstand the kind of groups that were coming. I'm just wondering, you know, what do you ascribe that to? Is it just kind of live and learn and, you know, everything you just, you know, you're open and then you gotta figure out what you have to do differently?
Is there something, you know, that you particularly kind of pinpoint this to, that you would have to put this much CapEx in when it's still a relatively new property?
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah, it's not a misunderstanding of the groups. You know, keep in mind that we were a minority partner in the Rockies through the construction period and then bought our partners out after opening. Really what we're doing with the Rockies is that we're taking essentially that Grand Lodge, which is the best real estate in that hotel, and converting it from areas that are seemingly not revenue producing and converting that square footage into space that is sellable that we can generate revenue by servicing groups. It will allow us to drive profitability, service more groups.
The Grand Pavilion is an expansion of meeting space, which really speaks to you know the demand that we're seeing there versus the original product that was built. This is... It's not that, you know, we misunderstood the market. I just think it really is more an issue of design and how that hotel was built, and how they used the sellable square footage to maximize the profitability of the asset.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Do you mind if I add to this? The other thing that our investors need to understand is prior to this hotel arriving in Colorado, there was not another convention resort in that state that you know drove really any material group room nights into that state. When we opened this hotel, as Mark said, we were a minority partner at the time. When we opened this hotel, you know, we had well over 1 million room nights on the books, of which the vast majority had never been to the state of Colorado before.
What we have discovered is that this market next to this airport is so attractive to the group consumer, and that is why we've been deploying this capital to make sure that this hotel, you know, once it's fully completed, and by the way, you know, we're looking at potentially adding 300-400 hotel rooms here. We're looking at, you know, a potential SoundWaves here. It's because of what we have discovered in terms of the appetite and desire of the group meeting planner to frequent this location. What we're trying to do with this hotel over time is create an asset that looks a little bit like, size-wise Opryland, that is so competitively superior. That is what we're doing here.
This is a very exciting asset in a very good market with extraordinary tax benefits that we have that really help generate very high returns on capital. If there are any members of our investment community that don't understand that, we're happy to help them. You know, I think Mark, the folks, Jennifer, the people that we meet understand that what we're doing here is repositioning this hotel into something that we believe will be quite extraordinary when it's completed.
Smedes Rose
Director, Citi
Great. Thanks for the answer.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thanks, Smedes.

That will conclude today's question and answer session. I'll now turn the call over to our presenters for any additional closing remarks.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I think we're done. No, no. Look, look, here, you know, we've done this earnings call this morning, but it's on the back of,
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
You know, a day and a half.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I feel like we've been doing.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
A day and a half of, you know, investor meetings we had just several weeks ago. I think, if we keep talking, we're just repeating everything that we've said over the last month. Thank everyone for being on the call this morning, and if you have any additional questions, please feel free to reach out to our IR folks or Jennifer or Mark, and we look forward to all the conferences that our team will be participating in over the next couple of months. Thank you, everyone.

Welcome to Ryman Hospitality Properties' Q1 2022 Earnings Conference Call. Hosting the call today from Ryman Hospitality Properties are Mr. Colin Reed, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Mark Fioravanti, President, Ms. Jennifer Hutcheson, Chief Financial Officer, Mr. Patrick Chaffin, Chief Operating Officer, and Mr. Scott Bailey, President, Opry Entertainment Group.
This call will be available for digital replay. The number is 800-925-9951, with no conference ID required. At this time, all participants have been placed on listen-only mode. It is now my pleasure to turn the floor over to Ms. Jennifer Hutcheson. Ma'am, you may begin.
Jennifer Hutcheson
CFO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Good morning. Thank you all for joining us today. This call may contain forward-looking statements as defined in the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including statements about the company's expected financial performance. Any statements we make today that are not statements of historical fact may be deemed to be forward-looking statements.
Words such as believes or expects are intended to identify these statements, which may be affected by many factors, including those listed in the company's SEC filings and in today's release. The company's actual results may differ materially from the results we discuss or project today.
We will not update any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events, or any other reason. We will also discuss non-GAAP financial measures today. We reconcile each non-GAAP measure to the most comparable GAAP measure in exhibits to today's release.
I'll now turn the call over to Colin.
Colin Reed
Chairman and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you, Jen, and good morning, everyone. Q1 of 2022 was one of the most remarkable quarters I've witnessed in this business, and I've been in it a long time. The rates of change from week to week and month to month as the Omicron variant receded and the group demand resurged, was unlike any other trajectory I'd seen, except perhaps for the earliest days of the pandemic, when the trajectory was essentially reversed.
Our hospitality portfolio went from 60 points of occupancy and $42 million of adjusted EBITDA in the month of December, down to 33% and less than $1 million in January as the Omicron impact was felt.
In February, it rose to 46% occupancy and nearly $17 million of EBITDAre, before, in March, reaching over 63 points occupancy and $52 million of adjusted EBITDAre. The pace of recovery exceeded our expectations as we anticipated it would be much harder to offset the Omicron cancellations in such a short window, as we discussed very clearly on our February earnings call.
There were two primary factors that helped deliver these results. One is the continued strength of our leisure transient business, which we have highlighted before. This trend carried over from the holidays through to a robust spring break season in March. Our leisure transient ADR grew 26% compared to Q1 2019, and 35% over Q1 last year.
The Gaylord Palms saw some of the largest spring break crowds, hosting 5,000 more transient room nights in Q1 of this year than in Q1 2019. In March, the Palms turned in their single best month's performance on record for revenue and adjusted EBITDAre. The hotel's Q1 was only $1.1 million below its Q1 2019 levels in profitability, despite 27 fewer points of occupancy due to the Omicron cancellations on the group side.
This was truly a remarkable performance. The other factor leading us to surpass internal expectations was the rapid recovery in group travel as the weeks went on. Now, to give you a sense of just how fast things were happening, we quite literally had groups who early in the quarter indicated that they were likely to cancel.
Then as things started to look better, their message became, "Well, we still plan to meet, but you should expect higher than normal attrition." As the meeting date arrived, some of these groups not only traveled, but exceeded their original blocks. Crazy times indeed. On the group side, we collected close to $20 million in cancellation and attrition fees, and since the beginning of the pandemic, we've collected now over $95 million in fees.
We feel very good about the strength of our contracts going forward as some of the last vestiges of the pandemic restrictions fall away, such as the airline mask mandate and travel truly normalizes. Looking ahead for our hospitality business, we feel confident that the momentum we experienced in Q1 will continue, barring an exogenous event.
To highlight this, at the end of Q1, our lead volumes were the highest they have been since the pandemic began, and only 4% below 2019 lead volumes, having added 2 million new leads in the 3 months in Q1. Within those leads, our near-term, in the year, for the year lead volumes continue to exceed 2019 levels.
In terms of production, the 422,000 gross group room nights booked in Q1 exceeded Q1 2019 by almost 7%. Now to help frame how impressive this is, consider that in the immediately preceding quarter, that is in Q4 2021, we booked nearly 1 million gross group room nights.
Typically, a large Q4 production number like that, like the one I just talked about, includes some amount of draining the funnel at year end. The following Q1 of the new year is more likely to see slower production as the funnel of new leads gets replenished. Our emphasis on driving future rate growth paid off handsomely in the Q1, with ADR on new group bookings 8% higher than in the Q1 of 2021, and 13% higher than the Q1 of 2019.
The value proposition we offer meeting planners through the investments that we have made in our portfolio over the last 5 years positions our hotels with a significant competitive advantage in terms of quality and volume of meeting space, variety and attractiveness of food and beverage outlets, renovated room product, and extensive and unique amenities.
All together, we feel very good about the trajectory our hospitality is on, as we exit the Q1, and the prospects for continued recovery in organic production, for both this year and future years. Now turning to our entertainment business, we saw a similar pattern of month-by-month improvements as Omicron abated.
If we set aside our investment in Circle and look at the wholly owned operating businesses in this segment, led by the Ryman Opry House and our Ole Red venues, these businesses started January at a loss of $1.1 million in adjusted EBITDAre. By February, as attendance recovered, they generated positive $2.3 million, and in March, turned in $6.4 million.
For this Q1 as a whole, these businesses reached $7.4 million of positive adjusted EBITDAre. On a same store basis compared to the Q1 2019 and thus excluding both Circle and Ole Red Orlando, which opened in 2020, this segment reached 93% of its Q1 2019 performance, even with the impact of Omicron in January and February.
Our big news in Q1 was that we have reached an agreement with Atairos and NBCUniversal to partner with them and sell 30% of our entertainment business at a minimum enterprise value of $1.415 billion, with the potential to climb to $1.515 billion if certain performance metrics are met in 2023 and 2024, with both valuations inclusive of the presumed closing of Block 21.
This agreement is a win all around for our shareholders, our employees, our customers, the artists that are on our stage, and our new partners. For starters, it sets a public valuation mark on this business, which we've long argued was undervalued by the market given the demand for live entertainment assets, especially ones as unique and irreplaceable as the Ryman Auditorium and the Grand Ole Opry House.
It provides a boost of liquidity to Ryman in the form of Atairos, roughly $290 million equity purchase, which will lower our combined leverage by nearly half a turn after fees and expenses, and helps accelerate our post-pandemic deleveraging plans. It brings the extensive expertise and strategic capabilities of Atairos and NBCUniversal to accelerate the reach and expand the growth opportunities of this business across live entertainment performances, content creation, and digital distribution.
It also creates scale, and thus new opportunities for our employees and new avenues and outlets for our artists and consumers to discover each other. It retains 70% of the upside of all of these opportunities for our existing shareholders with a clear set of options to eventually fully separate this business from the REIT, something we've always said was the best alignment for both businesses.
Now turning back to our hotel business just for a moment, let me talk briefly about the future. Here's where we get really, really excited. All of the proactive decisions that we have taken over the last few years, including product enhancements and expansion, group sales staff retention, and bringing in new folks to bolster our group sales processes, have all resulted in a really strong book of forward business and a very impressive leisure business.
As a consequence of all of this, the remainder of this year is shaping up to be remarkably strong. At the beginning of April of this year, we had over 524,000 net group room nights on the books for Q2, and approximately 1.4 million for the remaining 9 months of the year.
Now in terms of how these numbers compare to where we sat at the same time in 2019, here's what's interesting. As of 31 March of this year, our room nights on the books for the rest of 2022 represent 97% of 2019 group room nights on the books for 2019, but with an ADR growth of 8.6%.
By the way, when you look at the group room nights that we have on the books as of 31 March 2022 for the year of 2023, these represent 102% of the 2019 group room nights we had on the books as of 31 March of 2018. Again, with an ADR growth of 8.6%.
These are incredibly strong numbers, considering we just spent the last 2 years fighting a global pandemic. Now, Jen will share with you details of our guidance for the Q2 and the year, and you'll see, given the strength of our business, we're projecting that the next 9 months on a consolidated basis at the midpoint will exceed our 2019 performance from an adjusted EBITDAre perspective.
Now I'll stop here as I have both Mark and Jen joining me today, as Jennifer has now stepped into our Chief Financial Officer role. Jen, congratulations again on that. Mark's duties have expanded as President of the company, and congrats to you, Mark, as well. I'll turn over to them for additional comments, and then we'll open up the lines for questions. Mark?
Mark Fioravanti
President, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thanks, Colin. Now let me add a bit of color to the hospitality operational results for the quarter, particularly a snapshot of March, as it's the best indicator of where our business stands post Omicron. Colin indicated the rapid improvement in the quarter of group occupancy as we ended at 63% overall occupancy in the month of March. I would add that our group mix for the month of March was 70% of total room nights, and that compares to 76% of total room nights in March of 2019.
In January of this year, group was 61% of room nights traveled compared to 80% in January 2019. While the transient was very strong throughout the quarter, it was the group recovery that really closed the occupancy gap as the period went on.
Within those Q1 group room nights, our mix of corporate groups was 66% compared to 60% in Q1 of 2019. While early in the pandemic, recovery of corporates seemed the most hesitant to dive back in, we're happy to report that they're now coming back in numbers. Another positive trend in the quarter was the level of group outside the room spending.
For the full quarter, we saw about $229 of banquet spending per group room night, only 1.5% below Q1 of 2019. However, in March, that figure continued to improve and reached $254 per group room night, a 7.6% increase compared to March of 2019.
With the return of more corporate groups, we're pleased to see outside the room spending activity reach pre-pandemic levels as both leisure and groups are spending well on property. Quickly, a few trends by hotel. The Gaylord Palms had the steepest occupancy recovery month by month during the quarter, going from 27% in January to 79% in March.
Opryland also performed very well with leisure transient, picking up over 4,600 transient room nights compared to Q1 of 2019 and seeing over 32% growth in transient ADR over the same period. The group recovery was also pronounced at Opryland as total occupancy increased from 30% in January to 72% in March.
The Gaylord Texan was close behind these leaders, reaching 72% occupancy in March and also adding 3,000 transient room nights compared to Q1 of 2019. The Gaylord Rockies and Gaylord National were the two hotels where the pace of Omicron recovery was not quite as dramatic month by month within the quarter. The Gaylord Rockies gained 4,900 transient room nights compared to Q1 2019 and doubled occupancy from 27% in January to 54% in March.
As most of you know, the Gaylord National has the lowest leisure transient mix of our five Gaylord hotels. As such, the National did not benefit as much from the strong leisure demand recovery and continued to experience the lingering impacts from the Omicron variant on group room nights.
Overall, hospitality margins held up relatively well in the face of Omicron in the quarter, with adjusted EBITDAre margins off a modest 7 points year over year compared to Q1 of 2019, despite a 25-point decline in occupancy and a 21% increase in average wage rate over Q1 of 2019. Our emphasis on retaining key staff members is proving prescient as group business has returned in volume post the Omicron disruption.
We continue to believe that as occupancy recovers and high margin outside the room revenue streams return to these groups, the productivity measures we've implemented through the course of the pandemic will yield improved margins longer term compared to pre-COVID levels.
Looking ahead, our on the books position for the balance of the year looks very healthy, as Colin provided a snapshot of our group room nights on the books for Q2 and the rest of the year. Translating these figures to occupancy, as of 31 March, for the balance of this year, we had 48.4 points of net group occupancy on the books, down only 3.1 points compared to the same time in 2019 for the balance of the year.
The ADR for these group room nights is 8.6% higher than the same period in 2019, which means we have 5% more group rooms revenue on the books for the balance of the year than we did for the balance of 2019.
With our end of year for the year lead volumes also outperforming 2019, we feel very good about the rest of the year given this base of business and the momentum coming out of March. On the investments front, we're in the final stages of the assumption process with the CMBS servicer for Block 21 and anticipate a closing before 1 June.
We anticipate our strategic partnership with Atairos and NBCUniversal to close after the Block 21 transaction, but by the end of Q2. I'll now turn it over to Jennifer to provide a brief financial balance sheet and liquidity update along with our guidance.
Jennifer Hutcheson
CFO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you, Mark.
In Q1, the company generated total revenue of $299.1 million and a net loss to common shareholders of $24.6 million for a loss of $0.45 per fully diluted share. In terms of our balance sheet, net debt is approximately unchanged sequentially from the end of Q4 2021 at $2.8 billion.
The company had available liquidity of $638.4 million, consisting of $510 million of capacity under our revolving credit facility and $128.4 million of unrestricted cash. We effectively exited our covenant waiver period for our secured credit facility with the end of Q1.
Beginning with Q2, we will now once again be required to meet certain maintenance covenants in terms of consolidated fixed charge coverage and implied debt service coverage ratios. However, these ratios are modified to reduce thresholds, to reduce threshold levels of 1x and 1.1x respectively through the balance of 2022, and will be based on annualized results for that time.
All other special restrictions related to our pandemic covenant waiver are no longer in effect, such as limits on discretionary capital spending, acquisitions, investments, or debt incurrence. For the Block 21 transaction, we expect to assume approximately $137 million of CMBS debt on the property when the deal closes and expect to fund the balance of the $260 million purchase price with cash on hand or borrowings under the revolving credit facility.
Subsequent to the Block 21 closing, we expect to receive gross proceeds from the Atairos investment and the new $300 million OEG segment level Term Loan B of approximately $590 million before transaction fees and expenses, which we will use to retire our existing Term Loan A and outstanding amounts under our revolving credit facility.
We're currently making progress in the execution of the new Term Loan B for Opry Entertainment and expect to simultaneously place a $65 million revolving credit facility for this business, which will be undrawn at close, but available to support the business's growth with our new partners. The net results of this transaction, as Colin noted earlier, should be around a one half turn improvement in net leverage on a consolidated basis.
We will continue to prioritize both deleveraging post-pandemic and taking advantage of high-return reinvestment opportunities across our businesses with our free cash flow. Finally, given the momentum with which we exited the Q1, we are comfortable resuming the provision of guidance for the current year.
For this current Q2 of 2022, we expect our hospitality segment to deliver between $120 and 124 million of adjusted EBITDAre, and our consolidated company to produce $135 to 145 million of adjusted EBITDAre, including any partial quarter contributions from Block 21 subsequent to closing. For the full year 2022, we expect hospitality segment to deliver $425 to 440 million of adjusted EBITDAre.
Combining that with our corporate segment and our already published annual guidance for our entertainment business of $80 to 88 million of adjusted EBITDAre, which we issued last month in conjunction with the announcement of the Atairos investment, and which again includes the expected contribution of our pending acquisition of Block 21.
We expect the consolidated company to produce $476 to 502 million of adjusted EBITDAre this year. At the midpoint of $489 million, this would represent over 95% of our pre-pandemic 2019 full year adjusted EBITDAre of $510 million.
If you subtract our Q1 actual results, our guidance ranges for the balance of this year represent, at the midpoint, 98% of our 2019 performance for our hospitality segment and 106% for our consolidated company. With that, I turn it back over to Colin.
Colin Reed
Chairman and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you, Jen. Well done. Thank you, Mark. Chelsea, let's open up the lines for questions and see what's on folks' minds here this morning.
Operator
Yes, sir. At this time, if you would like to ask a question, please press the star and one on your touch-tone phone. You may remove yourself from the queue at any time by pressing the pound key. Once again, that is star and one to ask a question, and we'll pause for a moment to allow questions to queue. Our first question will come from Shaun Kelley with Bank of America Merrill Lynch.
Shaun Kelley (Bank of America Corporat
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst for Gaming, Lodging, and Leisure Equities
Hi, good morning, everyone. Thank you for all the detail and color, and congratulations on a really strong March. If we're going to start, maybe the best place I think would be to dig in on the revenue side a little bit. Appreciate all the clarity on guidance and the bottom line trajectory of where everything's at.
If we think about the mix of where you're at, I think the numbers given were 48.4% of net group room occupancy on the books, down about 3 percentage points and then up 5% overall on group room revenues. Can you help us think about how that translates into just the overall revenue or RevPAR picture for Ryman?
Just given that obviously there's still some work to be done on the balance of the year. What are some of your assumptions around kinda that book of business or what needs to be, what kinda needs to go in to fill in the gaps between here and the rest of the year?
Colin Reed
Chairman and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Right. So first of all, I think, Patrick, the reach we have is pretty limited. We're in really good shape on reach on group side for the year, given the tremendous book of business we have and particularly the rate. The other thing that we didn't really talk about as we think about the rest of the year is what is going on on leisure. You know, we are seeing leisure volumes.
How do I describe this? Very, very encouraging in terms of room nights, but extraordinarily encouraging in terms of the rate that we're booking these leisure room nights at. You know, Shaun, we feel really pretty good all around about right now. That's why we're, you know, prepared to give guidance for the year.
We feel very good about where we sit right now for this year. You wanna add to that, Patrick?
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Sure. Hey, Shaun, it's Patrick. To your point a minute ago, you know, we talked about the 48 points of occupancy. That's about 1.38 million room nights on the books from a group perspective.
If you add on to that just what we did in 2019 from a transient perspective, which was about 22 points of occupancy or 620,000 room nights, that would get you about 2 million room nights for the remainder of the year, which would imply around, you know, 70% occupancy for the remainder of the year as far as what we have on the books on group, what we expect to do on transient at a minimum.
We anticipate that we'll exceed the transient we did in 2019 because as you've seen over the past couple of years, we've gotten more savvy with our transient leisure programming. More and more folks have become aware of the unique offerings that our hotels have from a leisure amenity perspective. I expect we'll exceed the transient room nights.
If you say, okay, if they do nothing else on the group side, they're gonna be at, you know, roughly 70%. We anticipate that we'll obviously do a lot more, and on average, I would say we would book probably somewhere between 60,000 and 80,000 more room nights for the remainder of the year. That would give you a feel from the group side.
That would give you a feel for how much more we think we can still do. You know, then you add on to that the rate. Mark mentioned this a minute ago. We have room nights on the books from a group perspective that are up 8.6% in terms of rate growth over 2019. If you look at just what we did in Q1 on the leisure transient side, we saw a growth of 14% ADR in what actually traveled during Q1.
Room nights, if nothing else happened, we'd be in good shape. We expect obviously to outperform and continue to deliver more room nights on the group side and on the transient side, a great story, especially with what's going on on the rate side.

Shaun, I don't want to crow about this, but, you know, we've taken as a company a very different approach to what I think most of our competitors have done in terms of, you know, continuing to enhance the product through Omicron. You know, we've spent a lot of money on improving just the proposition.
I think we've also, you know, Patrick, on the hotel side, I think we work with Marriott and encourage them to be more creative on the programming side for leisure. I think all of this, you know, stands us in really good stead to beat 2019 this year, as Jen said.
If things happen the way I hope they happen, you know, maybe, you know, come in stronger. You know, our business looks really good right now.

No, clearly from the numbers, that seems to be the case. Then second, or follow-up question would just be, could you help us think a little bit about like maybe the ramp-up of Rockies and National Harbor? Obviously, you know, it's a little bit, you know, those two properties sound like they were a little bit behind the trajectory you're seeing in some of the other markets.
So how is either the pacing at those properties or, you know, the step function that you may expect to see? Because overall, clearly the portfolio is getting to levels that, you know, would rhyme with 2019.
Is that, you know, disparity between, you know, are some properties well above and those two are still trailing, or do you see those catching up meaningfully in the next couple quarters?
Colin Reed
Chairman and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
The latter. Let me say this. The reason why these two hotels are slower coming out of the gate is because they don't have the same, at this stage of their life. You've got to remember Aurora's 2.5 years old, and this hotel does not have the leisure amenity and amenities and the historical relationship with hundreds of thousands of customers that the other hotels have that have been open, you know, a long time.
We've been able to build a book of really strong leisure business in the Oprylands, the Texans, and the Palms. Now, we've got plans for that. I would say Aurora has shown, you know, some strength on the leisure side this year. The group book of business for Aurora looks extraordinarily good. Patrick, you may wanna touch on that.
In terms of Washington, you know, the hotel just doesn't have the same pool complex, massive food and beverage offerings that some of these other hotels do. Those are the things that we're fixing. You know, the Washington hotel relies more on group than it does on transient. It has its lowest transient is, this hotel is the lowest percentage of transient business. Again, we've got ideas and thoughts about how we, over time, will fix that issue.
The book of group business for Washington looks really, you know, good over the next few months. You wanna give some data on that, Patrick?
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. Let's just consider the markets first, right? In Q1, DC was ranked number 23 in the top 25 markets from an occupancy perspective. The DC market has struggled to get back, compared to some of the other cities across the country. You have a market phenomenon going on there, and it's not too different from what has happened in Denver.
DC is much harder hit, but Denver ranked from a RevPAR perspective, about 17 out of the top 25 markets. Both markets have been a little bit slower to come back, DC more pronounced. To Colin's point, you know, National depends more on the group side. I would tell you, as you look at the summer, they have a very strong book of business, and we're very encouraged by what we've seen there.
From a margin perspective, I'm very encouraged because, you know, as we've talked about, we took the COVID period to really make some positive changes at that hotel. We did a rooms renovation. We're doing a full renovation of our food and beverage outlets. From a margin perspective, you know, that helps on the margin side, the F&B is helping on the margin side, but we made some fundamental changes in our union contract that help us position the hotel to perform better.
It would, sort of, have handcuffs on it, and we've removed those handcuffs, so the hotel should perform much better, especially in the food and beverage outlets. We see the group book of business strengthening as we go into the summer. We're encouraged by that. We're very encouraged by how that hotel is performing on the margin side and the setup for success.
You know, for a union hotel, it's been hitting the top of the brand in terms of guest satisfaction. It's doing all the right things, and as that book of business is increasing on the group side, I think it's set up for success. On Rockies, to Collin's point, it takes 4 or 5 years for us to build the transient base on which you can drive transient demand into a hotel.
Because of COVID, that's been stunted a bit. We're very encouraged, and we know Rockies is gonna get there. If you look at this summer, they also have a tremendously strong book of business. You know, their summer will be above 80% occupancy throughout the summer.
Feel really good about where Rockies is heading and know that as transient builds, that hotel will be set up for future success, very much so.

Bill Crow
Managing Director, Raymond James
Hey, good morning, guys. Appreciate all the details so far. Question number one of two. Can you talk about the stability of the workforce from two different perspectives? I guess just staffing levels slash turnover would be one. Kind of where is labor cost from a stability perspective? Have we seen the biggest increases, or are those continuing?
Colin Reed
Chairman and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
You wanna take that?
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Sure. Hey, Bill. Let's take wage increase first. You know, we saw roughly 20% increase in the Q4. We saw about 21% wage increase in the Q1. It feels like the pace of increase has slowed a bit, and we're normalizing. You know, we think there'll be additional wage increases, but we don't think it'll be as dramatic an increase as what we saw in 2021.
We're getting a little bit more comfortable and better handle on how to forecast for the future from that perspective. From a staffing perspective, we've tried to stay ahead of this. We've been very aggressive in trying to get quality folks on staff, get them trained, and then use bonuses and other means to keep them in place.
I would say relative to our peers, we've been able to keep our turnover a little bit lower. From a staffing perspective, though, I would say we still have a little bit of room to go, given the levels of occupancy that we're projecting for the summer. We're getting aggressive.
Applicant flow has increased over the past 60 days, and so we're encouraged that we're gonna be able to get there. But I would say that we were probably at 75% to 80%, depending on the hotel, of the full level of staffing we wanted. I'm comfortable that we'll get to 95% or 100% here in the next, you know, 45 days.
Colin Reed
Chairman and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Remind Bill about the efficiencies around management, Patrick, to offset the increases that we've seen in frontline.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. You know, I wanna make sure we draw a clear comparison or a clear distinction here. On the front line, we are going to come back to the original levels of staffing. You know, those frontline stars in housekeeping and front desk. We'll go back to the original numbers.
But from a management perspective, we've driven some synergies into the business, putting in quality over quantity and not just throwing bodies at problems, but really using the COVID time to solve some of those issues so that we can be more efficient on the manager side. You know, we think that there's a long-term, probably at least 15% reduction in our management headcount as a result that will drive margin improvement into the business.
Bill Crow
Managing Director, Raymond James
Great. Appreciate that. The other question I had is really, what are you hearing from prospective groups for next year? Clearly the advanced bookings pace has been terrific. Are you getting any indication of concerns about economic growth slowing or recession, as you talk to prospective groups for next year?
Colin Reed
Chairman and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
We're seeing none of that. It's something that we, you know, monitor lead volumes. Patrick and his team engage, I mean, daily with these sales leaders. I think we see a lot of encouraging signals in our business. You know, this industry, Bill, is big and deep. There's just a ton of organizations across America that want to meet. We just need to continue to gnaw away and slowly, you know, build our share here the way we've been doing it.
You know, we've done it through the way we treat our salespeople, the recruitment of more salespeople, and the quality of our product and the quality of our service. You know, the- If we have a recession for 6, 9 months, whatever it may be, you know, you go back and look at what happened to us in 2009 and financial crisis.
You know, we, because of the quality of our business and the quality of our people, you know, we absolutely look at these periods of time, the likes of which we've just gone through, as a period of time where we can actually gain share. We think that's what we've done here. That's why we're as optimistic and confident, and we have this forward book of business. You know, if there is a recession, you know, I think we'll do just fine through it.
Patrick Chaffin
